newsitem.title: CHINA: BELGIAN BANK MAY SELL OFF SOME HK MORTGAGES.
newsitem.headline: BELGIAN BANK MAY SELL OFF SOME HK MORTGAGES.

text.p: Belgian Bank is considering joining the growing throng of Hong Kong banks bundling up loans to clear its balance sheet, the bank said on Thursday.
Philip Fung, credit manager at the bank, said the bank might sell off home loans from its Hong Kong branch.
"That is being considered," Fung said, adding that the bank needed to manage its property exposure.

The Hong Kong Monetary Authority (HKMA) requires banks in Hong Kong to keep their property exposure to the banking sector average of 40 percent or below, and Fung said Belgian Bank's exposure was close to 40 percent.
"If 40 percent is the level at which the HKMA do not want banks to exceed, then we'll think of ways to keep on growing without breaching the guidelines," Fung said.

"Securitisation is one way. If we don't do it now, we still have to think about doing it with the Mortgage Corporation," he said, referring to a new Hong Kong agency, set up to securitise mortgages, which will open its doors later this year.
After a hesitant start in 1994, Hong Kong's securitisation market has gathered steam in 1997.
Wing Hang Bank Ltd said recently it was looking at selling some mortgages.
Analysts also said Bank of East Asia Ltd had mandated UBS for a deal, and Dah Sing Bank Ltd was seeking an arranger for a US$200 million transaction.
Securitisation involves pooling assets like mortgages, and issuing debt securities to investors.
Principal and interest payments to investors come from the payments made by the householders on their mortgages.
"It's got to be the way to go," Nikko Securities analyst Steven Thompson said.
"It is convenient (and) there does seem to be more demand now than there was five years ago," Thompson told Reuters.
Several entities have recently sold off loans, including Sanwa Finance Hong Kong, Hong Kong Telecommunications Ltd, and Dah Sing Bank Ltd.
Analysts said mortgage securitisations allowed banks to write a mortgage, and onsell the mortgage while retaining the original customer for more lucrative business like credit cards.
"That's the way to do it," said ING Barings analyst Peter Redhead.
